extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, literary critics, and students of poetry/drama
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical principles for composing and judging tragedy and epic poetry: diction, plot unity, metre choice, use of the wonderful/irrational, and how to answer critical objections. Intended to guide authors and critics in producing or evaluating poetic imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety in modes of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a great matter to observe propriety in these several modes of expression, as also in compound words, strange (or rare) words, and so forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words and forms appropriate to the genre and occasion; attention to compound and rare words contributes to stylistic distinction. Examples: certain phrase orderings give distinction though not part of current idiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command of metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: But the greatest thing by far is to have a command of metaphor. This alone cannot be imparted by another; it is the mark of genius, for to make good metaphors implies an eye for resemblances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphorical skill is central to poetic excellence and not teachable in straightforward fashion; cultivate an eye for likenesses to generate effective metaphors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate word choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the various kinds of words, the compound are best adapted to Dithyrambs, rare words to heroic poetry, metaphors to iambic. In heroic poetry, indeed, all these varieties are serviceable. In iambic verse, which reproduces familiar speech, the most appropriate words are those which are found even in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match lexical register and word-formation to the poetic species: use compounds for dithyrambs, rare/ornamental words for epic/heroic verse, and common prose vocabulary for iambic (spoken) verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative (epic) plot unity: single action
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot manifestly ought, as in a tragedy, to be constructed on dramatic principles. It should have for its subject a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end. It will thus resemble a living organism in all its unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose narrative poems around one coherent, causally unified action that can be apprehended as a whole; avoid sprawling themes that lack single results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating excessively vast subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Homer never attempts to make the whole war of Troy the subject of his poem ... It would have been too vast a theme, and not easily embraced in a single view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a bounded portion of a larger story rather than the whole immense subject; detaching a single portion admits episodes while preserving unity and avoiding over-complication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of episodes to diversify narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: He detaches a single portion, and admits as episodes many events from the general story of the war—such as the Catalogue of the ships and others—thus diversifying the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include relevant episodes to vary pace and add dignity and mass, but keep them subordinate to the central action so unity is preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic poetic kinds and required parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry must have as many kinds as Tragedy: it must be simple, or complex, or 'ethical,' or 'pathetic.' The parts also, with the exception of song and spectacle, are the same; for it requires Reversals of the Situation, Recognitions, and Scenes of Suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing epic, consider its moral/structural type (simple/complex/ethical/pathetic) and ensure necessary plot devices (reversal, recognition, suffering) are present where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic diction and thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Moreover, the thoughts and the diction must be artistic. In all these respects Homer is our earliest and sufficient model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize both crafted ideas and language; judge poems on the artistry of their thought and verbal expression, using exemplary models (e.g., Homer) as standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale/length appropriate to unity
rubrics_metrics.description: As regards scale or length ... the beginning and the end must be capable of being brought within a single view. This condition will be satisfied by poems on a smaller scale than the old epics, and answering in length to the group of tragedies presented at a single sitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep narrative length such that the work's beginning and end can be apprehended together; excessively long works risk loss of unity unless carefully structured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic advantage from narrative simultaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: In Epic poetry, owing to the narrative form, many events simultaneously transacted can be presented; and these, if relevant to the subject, add mass and dignity to the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the narrative form's ability to present concurrent events to enrich the poem, but only when they are relevant and contribute to the central effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sameness of incident (satiety)
rubrics_metrics.description: For sameness of incident soon produces satiety, and makes tragedies fail on the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce variation (episodes, differing incidents) to sustain audience interest and avoid monotony; balance unity with variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of metre must fit the genre
rubrics_metrics.description: As for the metre, the heroic measure has proved its fitness by the test of experience. ... On the other hand, the iambic and the trochaic tetrameter are stirring measures, the latter being akin to dancing, the former expressive of action. Still more absurd would it be to mix together different metres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a metre that suits the scale and tone: heroic metre for epic grandeur (admits rare words/metaphor), iambic/trochaic for action/dance; avoid mixing metres within a great-scale narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet should minimize self-appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person, for it is not this that makes him an imitator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let characters and actions carry the poem's imitation; avoid intrusive authorial presence except for brief prefatory words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the wonderful and the irrational
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of the wonderful is required in Tragedy. The irrational, on which the wonderful depends for its chief effects, has wider scope in Epic poetry, because there the person acting is not seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ the wonderful/irrational to please and to produce poetic charm—more freely in epic narrative where absurdities pass unnoticed; ensure such elements serve the poem's effect and are plausibly integrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Accordingly, the poet should prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inventing events, choose those that though impossible feel probable within the poem's logic rather than unlikely-but-possible occurrences; plausibility within the poetic world matters more than strict factual probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude irrationality from the action itself
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic plot must not be composed of irrational parts. Everything irrational should, if possible, be excluded; or, at all events, it should lie outside the action of the play ... not within the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid irrational incidents occurring within the dramatic action; if irrationality is necessary, place it outside the main action or justify it so the audience accepts it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify introduced irrational incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: But once the irrational has been introduced and an air of likelihood imparted to it, we must accept it in spite of the absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an irrational element is included, work to render it believable within the poem's terms (impart an air of likelihood) so the audience accepts it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction elaborated in pauses, not during character expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The diction should be elaborated in the pauses of the action, where there is no expression of character or thought. For, conversely, character and thought are merely obscured by a diction that is over brilliant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve ornate or elaborate language for moments when it will not obscure character or thought; keep language clear during scenes of strong character/idea expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as imitator: three objects to imitate
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet being an imitator ... must of necessity imitate one of three objects,—things as they were or are, things as they are said or thought to be, or things as they ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging accuracy or intent, determine which mode of imitation the poet has chosen (actual fact, reported belief, or ideal) before calling something 'incorrect.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Language as vehicle: current, rare, metaphorical
rubrics_metrics.description: The vehicle of expression is language,—either current terms or, it may be, rare words or metaphors. There are also many modifications of language, which we concede to the poets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate diction recognizing permitted poetic license: poets may legitimately use rare words or metaphorical language depending on purpose and genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different standards of correctness across arts
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard of correctness is not the same in poetry and politics, any more than in poetry and any other art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply domain-sensitive standards: what counts as an error in one art or sphere may be acceptable in poetic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish essential vs accidental faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the art of poetry itself there are two kinds of faults, those which touch its essence, and those which are accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a fault undermines the poetry's essential nature (serious) or is a correctable accident (less severe); e.g., wrong imitation of the object vs technical inaccuracies not essential to poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent vs non-essential errors
rubrics_metrics.description: If a poet has chosen to imitate something, (but has imitated it incorrectly) through want of capacity, the error is inherent in the poetry. But if the failure is due to a wrong choice if he has represented a horse as throwing out both his off legs at once, or introduced technical inaccuracies in medicine, for example, or in any other art the error is not essential to the poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate errors of artistic capacity (which damage the work's essence) from incidental factual/technical mistakes (which can be corrected without abolishing the poetic effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Justifying description of the impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: If he describes the impossible, he is guilty of an error; but the error may be justified, if the end of the art be thereby attained ... If, however, the end might have been as well, or better, attained without violating the special rules of the poetic art, the error is not justified: for every kind of error should, if possible, be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow impossible elements only when they are necessary to achieve the poem's artistic ends; otherwise avoid them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative seriousness of factual mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: For example,—not to know that a hind has no horns is a less serious matter than to paint it inartistically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess factual errors by their impact on artistic quality: minor factual ignorance is less harmful than failures in artistic representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic replies to factual objections
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may perhaps reply,—'But the objects are as they ought to be': just as Sophocles said that he drew men as they ought to be; Euripides, as they are. ... Or, 'This is how men say the thing is.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow defenses based on chosen mode of imitation: idealized depiction ('as they ought to be'), realistic depiction ('as they are'), or conventional/reported depiction ('as people say').

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual evaluation of acts and sayings
rubrics_metrics.description: We must also consider by whom it is said or done, to whom, when, by what means, or for what end; whether, for instance, it be to secure a greater good, or avert a greater evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge utterances and actions in context (speaker, audience, timing, means, purpose) rather than in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve linguistic/dialectical difficulties by form or usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Other difficulties may be resolved by due regard to the usage of language. ... Or again, the question may be solved by punctuation ... Or again, by ambiguity of meaning ... Or by the usage of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When facing apparent errors or oddities, examine meter/accents, punctuation, ambiguity, dialectal usages, and alternative senses before condemning the poet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret apparent contradictions by examining sense and relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Things that sound contradictory should be examined by the same rules as in dialectical refutation whether the same thing is meant, in the same relation, and in the same sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disambiguate contradictions by checking whether terms are used with the same meaning/relationship; consult the poet's own statements or tacit assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics should avoid groundless assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics ... jump at certain groundless conclusions; they pass adverse judgment and then proceed to reason on it; and, assuming that the poet has said whatever they happen to think, find fault if a thing is inconsistent with their own fancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should avoid projecting one's own assumptions onto the text; base objections on careful interpretation, not fanciful readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five sources of critical objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Things are censured either as impossible, or irrational, or morally hurtful, or contradictory, or contrary to artistic correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When responding to criticism, identify which of these five charges is being made and answer accordingly (by appeal to artistic necessity, mode of imitation, language usage, or contextual factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Censure of irrationality or depravity requires inner necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of the irrational, and, similarly, depravity of character, are justly censured when there is no inner necessity for introducing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce irrational incidents or morally corrupt characters unless the plot or thematic necessity demands them; gratuitous depravity or irrationality is legitimately criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy attains the art's end more perfectly (concentrated effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy ... has vividness of impression in reading as well as in representation. Moreover, the art attains its end within narrower limits; for the concentrated effect is more pleasurable than one which is spread over a long time and so diluted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value concentrated, unified dramatic works for their intense pleasurable effect; when comparing genres, assess how well each attains its specific artistic end (tragedy often superior in concentrated effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid condemning entire art for bad histrionic performance
rubrics_metrics.description: This censure attaches not to the poetic but to the histrionic art; for gesticulation may be equally overdone in epic recitation ... Next, all action is not to be condemned any more than all dancing—but only that of bad performers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate faults of performance (acting, gesture) from poetic composition; poor staging or delivery does not necessarily indict the poem itself.
